name: Balanced Trees and Why They Balance
intent: Understand why a plain binary search tree turns into a linked list on sorted input, how rotations keep a tree's height near log n whatever the insert order, and why databases use wide B-trees instead of binary ones.
scenario: A service keeps 10,000 keys in an ordered map built as a plain binary search tree, and a nightly import feeds it keys in sorted order. Every key goes to the right of the last one: the tree is 10,000 levels deep, building it costs 49,995,000 comparisons and a lookup averages 5,000.50. The same keys in an AVL tree (a tree that rotates to stay balanced) give a height of 14, 123,617 comparisons to build, 12.36 per lookup, and cost 9,986 rotations. Random input would have spared the plain tree (height 34), which is why the bug only shows up with real data.
problem: A binary search tree promises O(log n) search by halving the candidates at each node, but only if the tree is bushy. The shape depends entirely on insertion order: sorted, reverse-sorted, alternating or nearly sorted input (timestamps, auto-increment ids, imports) makes every new key a leaf at the bottom of one long chain. Nothing breaks and every answer is still correct; the structure is simply a linked list with extra pointers, and the cost is O(n) per operation, O(n squared) to build. Self-balancing trees fix this by repairing the shape after every change, and B-trees go further by making each node wide, because on disk the number of levels is what you pay for.

howItWorks.title: Order decides the shape of a plain BST
howItWorks.text: A binary search tree keeps smaller keys on the left and larger on the right, so a lookup discards one subtree at each comparison. The tree is built by inserting keys one at a time, each as a new leaf, and no insertion ever moves an existing node. So the first key becomes the root whatever it is, and the shape is a record of the insert order. Random order gives a tree of height around 2 to 3 times log2 n (34 levels for 10,000 keys). Sorted order gives height n.

howItWorks.title: Count the damage
howItWorks.text: With 1,000 sorted keys the plain tree has height 1,000 and costs 499,500 comparisons to build, which is n times n minus 1 over 2. A lookup walks half the chain on average: 500.50 comparisons. The AVL tree built from the same keys has height 10, costs 8,977 comparisons and 8.98 per lookup. The "zigzag" order (1, n, 2, n-1, ...) looks shuffled to a human and is just as bad: height n again.

howItWorks.title: A rotation, in plain words
howItWorks.text: A rotation changes which of two neighbouring nodes is the parent, without changing the left-to-right order of the keys. If a node's left child is too tall, you promote that child: it becomes the parent, the old parent becomes its right child, and the child's former right subtree is handed to the old parent as its left subtree. Three pointers change, the in-order sequence is identical, and one level moves from the tall side to the short side. A rotation is cheap and local: no key is compared, no node is copied.

howItWorks.title: AVL and red-black: two ways to decide when
howItWorks.text: An AVL tree stores a height per node and rotates whenever the two sides of a node differ by more than 1 level (a double rotation fixes the bent case). That keeps the height within about 1.44 times log2 n, the tightest of the common schemes, so lookups are cheap, but inserts rotate often: 9,986 rotations for 10,000 sorted keys. A red-black tree colours nodes and rotates by looser rules, which allows a height up to about 2 times log2 n, but a single insert needs at most 2 rotations. The usual summary: AVL for read-heavy data, red-black as the general-purpose default, which is why many standard-library ordered maps use red-black trees. Both are O(log n) for search, insert and delete in the worst case.

howItWorks.title: B-trees: balance by width, for disks
howItWorks.text: A B-tree keeps hundreds of keys in each node, sized to a disk page, and splits or merges nodes to stay balanced, so all leaves are at the same depth. What matters on storage is how many pages a lookup reads, and the levels are log base fanout of n: for a billion keys a binary tree has 30 levels, a B-tree with 100 children per node 5, with 500 children 4. Binary trees win in memory where a pointer hop is cheap and nodes are small; B-trees win wherever a hop costs a page read. Database indexes are B-trees or close relatives, and LSM trees take a different route to the same problem.

pros: Guaranteed O(log n) search, insert and delete whatever the insert order
Keys stay ordered: range scans, nearest-key and sorted iteration come for free
A rotation is a handful of pointer changes, so repairing the shape is cheap
B-trees keep disk reads to a few pages even for billions of keys
cons: More complex than a hash map and slower for plain exact-match lookups
Every insert and delete pays bookkeeping (heights or colours, and rotations)
Pointer-based nodes are cache-unfriendly: a balanced binary tree is often slower in practice than a sorted array or a B-tree with the same step count
Writing your own is easy to get subtly wrong (delete especially), and almost never necessary
whenToUse: You need keys in order, ranges, floor and ceiling queries, with inserts and deletes mixed in
Input order is not under your control: imports, timestamps, auto-increment ids, user-chosen keys
An in-memory ordered map or set from the standard library, which is usually a balanced tree
On-disk indexes, where a wide B-tree keeps the page reads to a few
whenNotToUse: Exact-match lookups only: a hash table is simpler and faster on average
Static data that is built once and searched often: a sorted array and binary search is smaller and cache-friendly
Hand-rolling a balanced tree when the language already ships an ordered map
Tiny collections, where a plain array scan is as fast as any tree
pitfalls: Building a plain BST from data that arrives sorted or nearly sorted: timestamps, ids and imports are exactly that. It works in tests with random data and collapses in production
Assuming that a tree that looks shuffled to you is balanced: the zigzag order (smallest, largest, next smallest, ...) is just as bad as sorted order
Saying "a tree is O(log n)" without saying "balanced": for a tree whose shape you do not control the honest bound is O(n)
Comparing AVL and red-black trees by Big O alone: both are O(log n); the difference is constants, AVL's tighter height against red-black's fewer rotations
Using a deep binary tree for data on disk: each level is a page read, so 30 levels is 30 reads where a B-tree needs 4 or 5
Recursive code on a degenerate tree: a tree 10,000 levels deep can overflow the call stack long before it is slow
Shuffling the input as a fix: it works for batch loads (a randomized BST has expected height O(log n)), but you must hold all keys first, and it does nothing for ongoing inserts in arrival order

roles.label: Data feed
roles.description: Supplies keys in some order: sorted imports, timestamps, random, alternating.

roles.label: Plain BST
roles.description: Inserts each key as a new leaf and never moves a node, so the shape records the insert order.

roles.label: Self-balancing tree
roles.description: Checks the heights after each insert and rotates where one side is too tall.

roles.label: B-tree on disk
roles.description: Wide nodes sized to a page, splitting and merging to keep every leaf at the same depth.

quiz.question: A plain binary search tree is built from 1,000 keys that arrive in increasing order. Roughly what does one lookup cost?
options: About 10 comparisons, since a binary search tree halves the candidates at every step.
About 500: the tree is a chain, and a lookup walks half of it on average.
About 1,000,000 comparisons, since every lookup compares against every pair of keys in it.
About 100 comparisons, as sorted keys fill the tree evenly from both sides of the root.
quiz.explanation: Each increasing key becomes the right child of the last one, so the tree is a chain of 1,000 nodes (500.50 comparisons per lookup on average, 499,500 to build). The halving only works if the tree is balanced, and a plain BST does not rebalance.

quiz.question: What does a tree rotation do?
options: It sorts all of the keys again from scratch so that the tree can be rebuilt from nothing.
It copies the tallest subtree into brand new nodes, which restores the balance of the tree.
It re-parents two neighbouring nodes by moving a few pointers; key order is unchanged.
It swaps two keys' values, so that the smaller keys end up closer to the root of the tree.
quiz.explanation: A rotation is a local re-parenting: the in-order sequence of keys does not change, three pointers do, and one level moves from the tall side to the short side. No key is compared and nothing is copied, which is why keeping a tree balanced after each insert is affordable.

quiz.question: A database index must find one of a billion keys, and every level of the tree costs a read from disk. Why is a B-tree preferred over a balanced binary tree?
options: A B-tree needs no rebalancing at all, so that inserts into it are essentially free of cost.
A balanced binary tree cannot be stored on disk at all, only ever in main memory.
A B-tree stores its keys in no particular order, which makes writes a good deal cheaper.
Wide nodes cut about 30 levels to about 5, so a lookup reads a handful of pages.
quiz.explanation: Levels are log base fanout of n. With 100 or more children per node a billion keys need 5 levels or fewer, against 30 for a binary tree, and each level is a page read. B-trees still split and merge nodes to stay balanced, and they keep keys in order.
